```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 7)
```

Differential equations describe the average behaviour of a big population.
When only a few people are infected, chance matters: a single case may infect
nobody and the outbreak dies out immediately.

The **Reed-Frost** chain-binomial model captures this in discrete generations.
If $I_t$ people are infectious and each pair of people has probability $p$ of
a transmitting contact, a susceptible escapes infection with probability
$(1-p)^{I_t}$. So

$$ I_{t+1} \sim \text{Binomial}\big(S_t,\; 1 - (1-p)^{I_t}\big). $$

```{r}
reed_frost <- function(N = 200, I0 = 1, p = 0.01) {
  S <- N - I0
  I <- I0
  total <- I0
  while (I > 0) {
    new_I <- rbinom(1, S, 1 - (1 - p)^I)
    S <- S - new_I
    total <- total + new_I
    I <- new_I
  }
  total                             # total number ever infected
}

N <- 200; p <- 0.01
R0 <- (N - 1) * p                   # about 2
R0
```

# Run many outbreaks

```{r}
set.seed(42)
sizes <- replicate(500, reed_frost(N = N, p = p))

hist(sizes, breaks = 30, col = "grey80",
     xlab = "Total infected (out of 200)", main = "500 simulated outbreaks")
```

The histogram is **bimodal**: many outbreaks fizzle out early (minor
outbreaks), while others take off and infect a large part of the population
(major outbreaks).

# Probability of a minor outbreak

```{r}
mean(sizes < 20)                    # fraction of outbreaks that fizzled
```

Early in an outbreak, the number of new cases from each case behaves like a
branching process. The probability $q$ that it dies out solves
$q = e^{R_0 (q-1)}$:

```{r}
q <- uniroot(function(q) q - exp(R0 * (q - 1)), c(0, 0.999))$root
q                                   # theory
```

Even with $R_0 \approx 2$, roughly one introduction in five goes nowhere. The
deterministic SIR model cannot show this, which is why stochastic models are
important for small populations and early outbreaks.
